28o I. — The League of Nations in 1926. The year 1926 was marked by two events of far-reaching importance for the development and future of the League of Nations, namely, the admission of Germany as Member of the League and the re-organisation of the Council. These events took place in the midst of complications and difficulties which began in March at the special Assembly, and which were only settled in September during the Seventh Session of the Assembly. On September 8th, Germany was admitted to the League by unanimous vote, receiving a permanent seat on the Council. On the same occasion, in order to take account in a wider and more equitable measure of the principle of the geographical distribution of seats, the number of non-permanent seats on the Council was increased from six to nine. At the same time, the Assembly introduced new rules for the election, term of office and re-eligibility of the non-permanent Members of the Council. This system, with certain temporary provisions, was immediately put into force. Considerable progress was made in two important tasks undertaken by the League, namely, the preparation of a general conference for the reduction and limitation of armaments, and that of an international economic conference. The Preparatory Commission for the Disarmament Conference, on which twenty-one States, including the United States, are represented, is the central orga¬ nisation for all preparatory work in connection with the Conference. It studied during the year the military and economic aspects of the problem, which it referred to its technical Sub-Commissions. The Committee of the Council made a thorough examination of the question of security, which, since 1922, has always been consi¬ dered by League organisations as inseparable from that of disarmament. While seeking means of facilitating, in case of aggression, the rapid working of the scheme of mutual assistance provided for by Article XVI of the Covenant, the Committee of the Council studied methods and regulations for ensuring the rapid working of League organisations in case of emergency, as well as the practical possibility of preventive action on the part of the Council, thus emphasising the importance of the first paragraph of Article XI of the Covenant. The Preparatory Committee for the Economic Conference whose extremely varied membership ensured evenly balanced representation of the various interests in question, drew up the agenda of the Conference, classifying in general chapters the matters to be discussed. It gave special prominence to two classes of questions, on account of their intrinsic importance and the public interest in them at the present time, namely, commercial and tariff policy and international industrial agreements. The Committee also agreed upon the documentation to serve as a basis for the work of the Conference, and proposed May 4th as its date of meeting. The Council agreed to these proposals. In the political field, strictly speaking, no new questions were submitted, the matters dealt with concerning the termination of affairs previously considered by the League. The Mosul dispute was definitely settled by an agreement between the Turkish and British Governments, in accordance with the Council’s recommen¬ dation; the recommendations of the Council with a view to the settlement of the Greco-Bulgarian incident have been, or are being, executed. As regards the development of international law, technical and humanitarian questions, considerable progress was made. The Permanent Court of International Justice held one ordinary and one extraordinary session, in the course of which it delivered a judgment and an advisory opinion.
